table.title: Table
table.summary: Build tables around your own data flow and UI. OrbitTable handles query intent and selection so your app stays in charge of fetching, rendering, and product rules.
table.tagline: Start with the directive, then choose the plain renderer or your own markup. The state model stays the same, so the visual layer can evolve without a rewrite.
table.apiSummary: The API stays intentionally small: one directive, a query model, selection state, and a few commands your UI can call.

overviewSections.title: How to think about it
overviewSections.body: OrbitTable tracks query intent and selection. Your feature still decides how data is loaded, when it refreshes, and how rows are rendered.
points: The core package does not ship table markup.
It does not enforce in-memory sorting, filtering, or pagination rules.
Renderer packages stay thin because they only read state and call commands.

overviewSections.title: What your app still does
overviewSections.body: Your app keeps the parts that are closest to the product: data fetching, query persistence, analytics, and empty or error handling.
points: Translate OrbitTableQuery into backend parameters.
Feed rows, total, loading, and error back into the directive.
Choose whether the UI comes from a renderer package or your own markup.

overviewSections.title: What stays out of scope
overviewSections.body: The table core stays conservative on purpose so teams can drop it into very different design systems without fighting built-in opinions.
points: No data adapter layer or HTTP client choice.
No CSS, tokens, or design-system dependency.
No business filters or row action rules.

renders.description: Use it when you want a solid baseline or when your team plans to fork the markup without bringing in Material or DaisyUI.

renders.label: Material
renders.summary: A ready-made renderer for teams already working in Angular Material.
renders.description: The renderer only talks to OrbitTableDirective. Your feature still handles backend mapping, errors, and row updates.
requirements: Install Angular Material in the host app.
Keep the same table wiring you would use with any other renderer.

renders.label: Daisy
renders.summary: A renderer for Tailwind + DaisyUI stacks that want to move quickly.
renders.description: Use it when DaisyUI is already part of your app and you want to adopt ng-orbit without inventing table markup on day one.
requirements: Install Tailwind + DaisyUI in the consuming app.
Keep query changes and data loading in the parent feature.

renders.label: Build your own
renders.summary: Own the markup while still letting OrbitTable handle state and intent.
renders.description: This is the long-term path when your product has a distinct visual language or cell layouts that a renderer package should not own.
requirements: Render your own table, grid, or card layout.
Call controller commands from the UI layer and keep product rules in the feature.

wizard.title: Wizard
wizard.summary: Build multi-step flows without giving up control of forms or layout. orbitWizard tracks navigation, progress, and completion while your app handles the real work.
wizard.tagline: Use the directive for flow state, then pair it with your own forms or a renderer package when you want a faster UI starting point.
wizard.apiSummary: The public API stays focused: one directive, a step model, and a small set of commands for moving through the flow.

overviewSections.title: How to think about it
overviewSections.body: OrbitWizard keeps navigation state, visited steps, completion rules, and validity tracking in one place. Your app still owns the forms, fields, and side effects.
points: The core package makes no CSS or design-system assumptions.
It does not generate forms or own your fields.
Optional renderers stay focused on UI composition.

overviewSections.title: What your app still does
overviewSections.body: Your app decides how each step looks, when data is saved, and which validations should block the next move.
points: Provide the step definitions.
Sync form validity into the controller.
Handle submit, autosave, analytics, and route guards at the feature level.

overviewSections.title: Why the kit helps
overviewSections.body: Many wizard flows already live on top of Angular forms. OrbitWizardStepFormSyncDirective keeps that form validity in sync with the headless state so you do not have to wire it by hand every time.
points: The directive is optional, but it is handy for form-backed steps.
You can still call wizard.setValid(stepId, valid) manually if you prefer.
Renderer packages should never own your submit rules.

adapters.title: Adapters

heroBlocks.title: Guiding principles
heroBlocks.code:
Keep the adapter thin.
Read UI state from the headless controller.
Turn UI events into controller commands.
Leave data fetching, forms, and side effects in the feature layer.

heroBlocks.title: Package map

adapters.summary: Adapters are the thin layer between ng-orbit state and your product UI. Build your own when you need it, or start faster with the Material and Daisy renderer packages that already ship today.
adapters.tagline: The rule stays simple: the controller owns state and commands, the adapter turns that state into UI, and your feature keeps data, forms, and business logic.
adapters.overviewCodeSectionLead: These renderer packages already exist, so you can move quickly now and still swap the UI layer later.
adapters.apiSummary: This page explains the integration contract behind adapters: what you read from controllers, what you send back through commands, and what should stay outside the adapter layer.

overviewSections.title: What adapter means in ng-orbit
overviewSections.body: An adapter is the UI-facing layer that reads controller state, maps it into your design system, and sends user intent back through controller commands.
points: An adapter can be as small as a custom template around an exportAs controller.
The ready-to-install Material and Daisy renderer packages are adapter flavors that already exist today.
The headless controller stays the single source of truth for UI state.

overviewSections.title: When to build one
overviewSections.body: Build a custom adapter when your product already has strong UI primitives, layout rules, analytics hooks, or accessibility patterns that a generic renderer should not own.
points: Wrap your own table, cards, step nav, or footer actions in a thin layer.
Keep that adapter reusable inside your product, not inside the core package.
Reach for the ready-to-install Material or Daisy packages when speed matters more than bespoke UI control.

overviewSections.title: Where kits and renderers fit
overviewSections.body: Kits help you compose product-owned UI without giving up the contract. Renderers package more UI up front, but they should still stay presentation-only.
points: wizard-kit is the current public bridge for form-backed wizard steps.
Table and wizard already have installable Material and Daisy renderer packages.
table-kit and wizard-render-plain still exist only as repo placeholders.
Renderers are optional and should not fetch data or own submit rules.
The same ownership rules apply whether the adapter is custom, kit-assisted, or a full renderer.

apiGroups.title: Core entry points
apiGroups.description: Adapters always begin from the public headless surface.

entries.description: Expose the table controller as exportAs="orbitTable" and read rows, query, selection, and commands from it.
Expose the wizard controller as exportAs="orbitWizard" and build your own step nav, progress UI, and footer actions around it.
Optional helper for form-backed wizard adapters when Angular form validity should drive the controller.

apiGroups.title: Read model
apiGroups.description: Adapters read normalized controller state and map it into product UI props.

entries.description: Use these signals to drive grids, cards, filters, pagination, and selected-state visuals.
Use these signals to render step chips, summaries, progress bars, and button disabled states.

apiGroups.title: Commands and events
apiGroups.description: Adapters send user intent into the controller and let the feature react to emitted events.

entries.description: Use commands for interaction, then let the parent feature react to normalized query or selection outputs.
Adapters trigger navigation and validity changes, while your feature decides what completion actually means.

apiGroups.title: Ownership boundaries
apiGroups.description: A healthy adapter is presentation-focused and easy to swap.

entries.description: Map controller state into product components, turn UI events into controller commands, and package reusable visual composition for the host app.
details: Layout, spacing, classes, and product-specific UI primitives belong here.
The adapter may normalize product event shapes before calling controller commands.

entries.description: Data fetching, backend mapping, form ownership, submit side effects, analytics, and business validation rules stay in the consuming feature.
details: Do not hide API calls inside the adapter.
Do not move wizard submit logic or table business filters into the UI layer.

renders.label: Headless custom markup
renders.summary: Read controller state directly and render product-owned HTML or UI primitives.
renders.description: This is the most flexible adapter style. It works well when your app already has a design system and you want ng-orbit to stay behind the scenes as the state contract.
requirements: Use the headless directive directly in the feature or adapter component.
Map clicks, search, paging, and step navigation to controller commands only.

renders.label: Kit-assisted composition
renders.summary: Add helpers when they reduce repeated wiring, while layout and styling still stay product-owned.
renders.description: wizard-kit is the current public example of this pattern. It bridges Angular form validity into orbitWizard while your adapter still controls markup, order, and interaction design.
requirements: Keep the final layout in your app or adapter component.
Use kit directives as composition helpers, not as a new home for business logic.

renders.label: Ready-to-install renderer adapters
renders.summary: Use the Material and Daisy renderer packages when you want a faster adoption path without building the first adapter yourself.
renders.description: These packages already exist for table and wizard. They depend on the same controller contract, but package the first layer of UI for teams that want to install and integrate quickly.
requirements: Table: @ng-orbit/table-render-material and @ng-orbit/table-render-daisy.
Wizard: @ng-orbit/wizard-render-material and @ng-orbit/wizard-render-daisy, plus @ng-orbit/wizard-kit for form sync.
Treat each renderer as a presentation layer and keep the same controller wiring so it stays swappable.

notes: You can start today with a renderer package and replace it later with a custom adapter because the controller contract does not change.

examples.label: Custom wizard UI
examples.title: Build a custom step layout on top of orbitWizard

examples.label: Form sync

examples.description: When your adapter renders wizard forms, wizard-kit can push Angular form validity into the controller without moving submit logic into the UI layer.
notes: Use wizard-kit as a bridge only. Submit, autosave, and analytics still belong to the consuming feature.
